The photo shows at night in her kitchen the grandmother stands at the step trash can, her foot on its pedal holding the lid open, a plate and fork in her hands, the white ceramic crock of teal silicone utensils on the counter beside the old white gas range. The grandmother: a 71-year-old Black American woman with medium-deep brown skin and warm undertones, a round face, short tapered silver-white coily hair, gold-framed reading glasses hanging on a chain at her chest, small gold earrings and a small gold cross. She wears a copper-colored silk blouse, a pearl necklace, a cream cardigan and a floral cotton apron. Every hand has five fingers in natural proportion and a natural grip; each person has exactly two arms and two hands; nothing floats. Everyone's eyes stay off-lens; nobody looks into the camera. Look: night, the kitchen lit only by the warm yellow range-hood light, the rest of the room falling into soft shadow, quiet and tense. Skin as a real camera sees it from a couple of meters away: natural, with subtle texture and slight unevenness, not retouched, not over-detailed; no airbrushed, waxy or plastic skin. Brown skin true to life: each person keeps their own skin depth and undertone, with soft natural highlights and visible detail in the shadows; palms lighter than the backs of the hands; never grey, ashy or lightened. Final check: the grandmother is the same woman as in her character sheet, with the same skin tone, silver hair, glasses on the chain and gold jewelry. No subtitles, no captions, no on-screen text.
